chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Hammad ibn Isa, from 'Asim al-Kuzi, who said:

I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) mentioning from his father that the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) performed the 'Aqeeqa for Al-Hasan (peace be upon him) with a ram, and for Al-Husayn (peace be upon him) with a ram, and gave something to the midwife, and shaved their heads on the seventh day, and weighed their hair, and gave silver in charity equal to its weight.

He (the narrator) said, So I said to him, 'Should the blood be taken and the head of the infant smeared with it?' He said, 'That is Shirk (associating partners with God).' I said, 'Glory be to Allah, Shirk?' He said, 'Even if that were not Shirk, it was practiced in the Pre-Islamic period (Jahiliyyah) and was forbidden in Islam.'

key_terms.شِرْكٌ: Polytheism or associating partners with God
key_terms.عَقَّ: To perform the Aqeeqa sacrifice for a newborn
key_terms.كَبْشٍ: A ram or young male sheep

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on smearing an infant's head with blood during Aqeeqa according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Kafi establishes the Sunnah of Aqeeqa for the Ahl al-Bayt, linking the Prophet’s actions to the purification of his lineage through specific rituals like shaving and charitable weighing of hair. Scholarly context emphasizes the distinction between the prescribed Islamic act of charity and the pre-Islamic (Jahiliyyah) practice of smearing the head with blood, which Imam al-Sadiq identifies as Shirk due to its pagan origins. This reinforces the Shia emphasis on purifying rituals from cultural syncretism while honoring the unique status of the Imams.
